<store>
Name: Fernhill Coffee Supply
Sells: Fernhill Coffee Supply sells home coffee brewing equipment and coffee beans. The range covers pour-over gear (ceramic and stainless steel drippers, size 02 paper filters, stovetop and electric gooseneck kettles, and a brew scale with timer), immersion brewers such as a French press and a cold brew jar, and manual and electric burr grinders. It also sells single-origin coffee beans from Fernhill Roastery in 250 g and 1 kg bags, whole bean or ground.
Audience: People who brew coffee at home, especially by pour-over or immersion, and who want to grind, weigh and control water temperature themselves. Some products, such as the single-dose flat-burr grinder and the temperature-hold kettle, suit buyers who care about precise brewing.
Tone: expert
Never say: —
</store>

content.text: {"title":"How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Ratio, Grind and Steep Time","angle":"The reader will learn what cold brew is, the coffee-to-water ratio, grind size and steep time that work, a step-by-step method in a dedicated jar or a French press, and how to choose beans and serve the concentrate.","sections":[{"heading":"What cold brew is, and why time replaces heat","covers":"Cold brew is an immersion method: coarse coffee steeps in cold water for many hours instead of minutes in hot water. This gives a smooth, low-bitterness concentrate. It also explains how cold brew differs from iced coffee.","facts":["F2","F10"]},{"heading":"What you need","covers":"Equipment checklist: a vessel with a filter, a burr grinder that can grind coarse, a scale, cold filtered water and fresh beans. Introduces the Cold Brew Jar as the dedicated option.","facts":["F1","F3","F4","F5","F8"]},{"heading":"Ratio and grind size","covers":"A starting concentrate ratio of about 1:10 coffee to water (150 g to 1.5 litres), and why a coarse, French-press-level grind matters. Fines make the brew muddy and over-extracted. The Hand Grinder covers this coarse range, but its hopper holds 25 g, so 150 g means grinding in about six loads. For larger batches, browse the grinder collection.","facts":["F6","F7","F26","F27","F28","F25"]},{"heading":"Step by step: making cold brew in the jar","covers":"1. Weigh and grind the coffee. 2. Fill the filter basket. 3. Pour cold water slowly to wet all the grounds. 4. Seal the jar and refrigerate. 5. Steep for 12 to 18 hours. 6. Lift out the basket and let it drain. Shorter steeps give a brighter brew; longer steeps give a heavier one.","facts":["F5","F8","F9","F10"]},{"heading":"No dedicated jar? Using a French press","covers":"The same method in a French press: steep coarse coffee in the fridge, then press and decant so the coffee stops extracting. The 1 litre capacity means scaling the recipe down to about 100 g of coffee per litre.","facts":["F52","F53","F58"]},{"heading":"Choosing beans for cold brew","covers":"Cold extraction mutes acidity and brings out sweetness and chocolate. Medium roasts with caramel and chocolate notes are a reliable choice. Colombia Huila is a strong match, and the 1 kg bag suits regular batches. Fruit-forward light roasts can also be used for a brighter cup.","facts":["F20","F22","F11","F14","F15"]},{"heading":"Diluting, serving and storing","covers":"Dilute the concentrate roughly 1:1 with water or milk over ice and adjust to taste. Keep it sealed and cold, and use it within about a week. Covers serving ideas and how to troubleshoot a sour or bitter batch.","facts":["F7","F8","F9"]}],"products":["P1","P2","P3"],"links":["P1","P2","P3","L1","L2","L3"]}
